prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength trapping scheme that allows many atoms to be interrogated free of Doppler and recoil shifts to its realisation at fractional uncertainties of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B015 as a single-part prize to Katori and Ye. After the full first round the case has survived the objection every supporter, including me, recorded, namely lineage against the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. My answer to the chair's question of what is new is one sentence: the magic-wavelength condition makes the light shifts of the two clock levels cancel, so a large ensemble of neutral atoms can be held and interrogated at once with Doppler and recoil effects removed, which turns the signal-to-noise problem of a single ion into a statistical one and is the reason the 10^-18 regime became reachable. Neither earlier prize covered that mechanism; the comb supplies the frequency ruler and the 2012 work the single-quantum-system control, and the lattice clock uses neither as its central idea. The mechanism is simple and general, it was analysed carefully, and it has been verified by direct comparisons between independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE), so the result is understood and not merely reported. Demonstrated uses, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift in a single sample and tighter limits on varying constants, show the device is already an instrument of discovery. I would keep the pending redefinition of the second out of the citation as supporting evidence: it is timing, not a bar, and it is not a reason to wait a year.
statement.case_against: This is still the most contestable point. A critic can say that going from 10^-15 to 10^-18 is an increment and that metrology is a tool rather than a discovery; I think the magic-wavelength scheme answers this, but the committee should say plainly that the citation rests on that scheme and not on the number. The two-name credit leaves out Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, and no member has produced a better pair within the statutes, so I accept the limit and flag it. My own first choice, the cavity method (B006), is in my view the more universal idea, but it has one supporter and a close overlap with the 2021 prize, so I do not carry it forward as a preferred part. A second part is not workable: any three-name partner added to B015 exceeds the three-person limit, and I do not think a second part is needed.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps topological insulators (B051) as his preferred part with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, concedes that Mele's omission and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal are the weak point, and asks whether the Kane-Mele pairing can be split. He lists B015 as an alternative.
responses.response: I do not think the pairing can be split. Kane and Mele wrote the Z2 classification together, and a citation that credits the theory but names only one of them would not survive scrutiny. My own trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp has the opposite defect: it drops Hasan, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that told Molenkamp what to measure sits outside any three names. That is why I keep B051 as an alternative and not as my choice. I agree with you that the physics is secure and mature, and I note that you say you would support B015 if the attribution cannot be resolved. On the evidence of this round it cannot be resolved within three people, so I ask you to treat B015 as the position that can be defended in full.

responses.point: Lindroth, with Kroll asked to draft the wording, ranks B015 first on the magic-wavelength cancellation of light shifts, and wants the committee clear about what is new relative to the 2005 and 2012 prizes and whether to await the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree with her reading of the mechanism and propose the citation wording above, which names the magic-wavelength scheme and the 10^-18 regime and avoids both the comb and the ion-control language. On the second I would rather not wait. A prize that rests on demonstrated clock-to-clock agreement at 10^-18 is already defensible, and tying it to an SI decision would make the Academy's timing depend on a metrology body. I would welcome her view on whether Lemonde and Pfau's early lattice work changes the credit; I cannot judge it from memory and do not want to claim more than I know.

responses.point: Kroll notes the strongest objection is lineage against Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012), and that the case rests on a two-orders-of-magnitude step plus the magic-wavelength lattice, with NIST, PTB, SYRTE and Lemonde not credited. He also discloses a Boulder lineage with Ye's group.
responses.response: I agree that the lineage is the real test, and I would not rest the case on the two orders of magnitude alone, as I said in round 1. The new element is the scheme, which is a mechanism, and the precision follows from it. On the uncredited groups I take his point that a purist can call this a tool, but I would not let that reasoning exclude measurement prizes in general, since the 2005 and 2012 prizes were exactly this kind. I note his disclosure of the Boulder tradition; it is a lineage, not a collaboration, and I do not think it needs recusal, though the committee should record it.

responses.point: Olsson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B017), accepts that the pairing mechanism is unresolved and that Yuan Cao and others are outside the credited names, and says she would not oppose B015 if the committee prefers a metrology prize.
responses.response: I still find the Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction the kind of simple mechanism I trust, and I agree that the reproduction across many groups is a real argument. My difficulty is the one she names herself: the origin of the superconductivity and the effect of twist-angle disorder are open, so the central phenomenon is not yet understood, and the experimental credit already needs Cao. I would revisit B017 in a few years. Her question whether B015 is a discovery or an invention in the statutory sense is fair; I answer that the magic-wavelength lattice is an invention in the sense of the statutes, and that it has produced measurements of nature, such as redshift within one sample, that were not possible before.

responses.point: Pearce, who moved from IceCube (B040) to B015, relies on Lindroth and Kroll for the technical judgement and asks whether Halzen alone can be defended, or whether a second or third IceCube or AMANDA name is needed.
responses.response: I agree with his move, and I appreciate that he treats the novelty question as one to be settled by the atomic-physics members. On B040 my position is unchanged: the diffuse flux is firm, but the credit to one name for a collaboration-scale discovery and the still-developing source identifications make it hard to defend this year. If it is carried forward, I think a defensible AMANDA or detector co-builder name has to be established first, and I do not see one within three names that is clean. I therefore see B040 as a case for later, not a part of a final configuration.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers a two-part prize pairing B015 with B040 (Halzen) for three laureates in total, values both as an instrument built to read a clue from nature, and concedes that single-name IceCube credit is the weak point.
responses.response: I take the argument that both are instrument-led achievements, but I do not think the pairing helps B015 and I would not add the second part. It would couple a case I regard as defensible to one he himself calls arbitrary in its credit, and it would make the prize look like a compromise between unrelated fields. I prefer to ask the committee whether B015 holds on its own, and my answer is that it does. If experts can establish an acceptable IceCube credit within the limit, I would reconsider in a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice with many-atom interrogation as a new mechanism, distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.

Whether Katori and Ye alone fairly represent the lattice clock given Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups; I cannot assess the early credit independently and rely on memory.
Whether B015 has gathered support because it is the safest choice rather than the strongest, which is the chair's observation about movement in round 1.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second is better treated as timing or as a reason to wait, which I regard as a judgement and not a scientific point.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B015: I have no known collaboration with Katori or Ye and no tie to the lattice-clock groups. I note Kroll's disclosed Boulder lineage, which I regard as a lineage and not a conflict. For B006, my profile shows no link to Mezard or Zecchina, though I work in neighbouring statistical-physics areas. Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson are in the Gothenburg physics environment, but no specific collaboration is recorded.
